summary:
Red Ledger is a walk map and helmet display for one Marswalk in Gale crater, at the boxwork ridges (a net of rock ridges) on Mount Sharp. It layers NASA data from several missions on one patch and prices each route in energy used, body heat stored against NASA's limit, radiation dose, and energy left to walk home.

Why it matters: on the day modelled, a radio signal took 20 minutes to reach Earth. A crew cannot ask and wait. It has to know, before it leaves, what each stretch of ground should cost the body.

The main result: on Mars the air can drop to -100 °C, and what stops a walker is their own body heat. Walking at 1 m/s on flat ground with no load, a person in a spacesuit makes 436 watts of heat and the suit removes 370. So the map plans the walk around heat: it places rests and compares routes by them. A visitor can click any ground to plan a walk there and back, see how far a body can go with no rest, and change the suit's cooling to see the plan change.

Before the body model was trusted, it was tested against NASA's measurements of people in spacesuits, with the pass mark fixed in advance. People used 36% more energy than it predicted. It was corrected by that rule, and every heat number now shows its range.
details:
Try it: https://red-ledger-mars.github.io/red-ledger/ · Code: https://github.com/Red-ledger-mars/red-ledger

What it does

Examine. Seven kinds of NASA data sit on one patch of 1.5 km by 1.9 km: imagery at 0.3 m per pixel, ground heat, elevation, radiation, weather, relay orbiter positions, and Curiosity's own path and photos. A 3D view shows the walk on the real terrain.

Diagnose. Four walks go from a habitat and back, each with a science goal at a place where Curiosity drilled or climbed; one adds ground the rover never reached. The planner finds the shortest route, and the route that costs the least walking energy, which refuses ground steeper than 24 degrees. Four readouts follow the walker: energy, body heat, radiation dose, and energy left to walk home. Near NASA's heat limit, the plan adds a rest.

Use it. Click up to four points and the page plans that walk in one to two seconds. The Reach layer colours every 4 m of ground by the rests needed to walk there and back. A slider sets the heat the suit removes, from 300 to 600 W, and prices the routes again.

Read it. "The Bill" tells one walk as a bill, cost by cost: the heat building up, the three rests, the two routes, the better suit, the test.

Check. The page writes a walk brief (before, during, after) with 13 checks NASA publishes for a spacewalk. The forecast can be downloaded, so a suit system can compare what the body does with what the ground should cost.

How it works

Walking energy comes from measurements at Earth gravity (Minetti et al. 2002), scaled to Mars gravity (Farley and McMahon 1992; an assumption) and multiplied by 1.364 for the suit. Work above the suit's cooling (370 W, a NASA prototype) is stored as body heat, against NASA's limit of 3.0 kJ/kg. Radiation and radio contact come from Curiosity's measured dose, NASA/JPL Horizons orbiter positions and the terrain.

The test against NASA's measurements of people

The test and its pass mark (within 15%) were committed before any measurement was collected (commit ea6f315; the result is b6f9b1d). The data are 40 NASA measurements of people on a treadmill at Moon and Mars gravity, 19 of them in a spacesuit, read from the reports and checked a second time.

  • Level ground: the model failed. People in the suit used 36% more energy than predicted. It was corrected by the rule, and the spread is the range on every heat number.
  • Climbs: it failed the other way, predicting up to 2.2 times too much. The slope cost is now scaled by gravity.
  • After the fix it is within 14% of all 12 sloped measurements. The fix came after seeing them: consistency, not a blind prediction.

Also checked: the shielding map against Curiosity's measurements (6 of 8 within 1 point) and the orbiter passes against a second computation (within 1 minute).

Results

  • On flat ground at 1 m/s the walker reaches NASA's heat limit after 60 minutes with no load, and after 28 minutes carrying 30 kg.
  • Carrying 30 kg, the direct route (2.25 km) would store 5.6 kJ/kg with no rest (range 3.8 to 7.7): 3 rests, 65 minutes. The body-cost route is about 100 m longer: 2 rests, 57 minutes.
  • The suit decides more than the route. On that walk, the body-cost route needs 4 rests if the suit removes 300 W, 2 at 370 W and none at 450 W. The route changes the count by one rest at most.
  • With no rest, a walker can go 630 to 1,140 m from the habitat and return with no load, and 490 to 700 m carrying 30 kg.
  • Walking slower can replace the rests. With 30 kg on the direct route, a steady 0.73 m/s needs no rest: 54 minutes against 65. The page marks this as an assumption, because NASA measured suited walking at Mars gravity at 1.12 and 1.34 m/s only. If walking slower costs 16% more energy per metre, the rests are as fast.
  • Leaving at 11:12 Mars local time, a relay orbiter is in view for the whole walk; at 13:47, for almost none of it.
  • One walk adds 23 to 31 microsieverts, under 0.01% of NASA's career limit.

Limits

The model is corrected from people in one suit on a treadmill, and no sloped test was at Mars gravity. The terrain is 4 m per cell, so the map cannot see single rocks. The habitat position and one stop are assumptions, marked on screen. The heat forecast itself is not tested on people. It is a planning forecast, not a diagnosis.

How it was built

Built with JavaScript, Leaflet and three.js. The code is open under the MIT licence. An AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) wrote the code, and collected and rechecked the data, under the team's direction. The idea and the decisions are the team's.
